sections.label: Inner Life
sections.description: What makes a life feel good to inhabit: meaning, freedom, connection, attention, emotional range, and the inner weather beneath everything else.

sections.label: Environment
sections.description: The settings, people, work, light, noise, nature, screens, and chronic inputs that a human system is continuously responding to.

sections.label: Rhythms & Recovery
sections.description: Simple ways I help the system find a useful pace, downshift, recover, and remember the difference between day and night.

sections.label: Movement
sections.description: Capability, strength, walking, conditioning, and movement that keeps life expansive rather than turning the body into a project.

sections.label: Food
sections.description: Food matters. Food is not everything. My bias is broadly bioenergetic, flexible, and allergic to making diet a religion.

sections.label: Frontiers
sections.description: Ideas I think deserve more attention. Some I’m fairly convinced by; others I’m still trying to understand.

entries.title: A Life Worth Inhabiting
entries.summary: My health model starts with the life being lived—not with perfect sleep, food, exercise, or supplements.
entries.currentTake: Psychoemotional and psychospiritual wellbeing feel like the largest lever. Meaning, connection, freedom, attention, and an honest relationship with myself change the context in which every physical intervention operates.
supportingDetails: Physical and inner wellbeing move in both directions.
Feeling alive is a better north star than becoming perfectly optimized.

entries.title: Freedom Is Physiological
entries.summary: A life that continually feels trapped will eventually be felt by the body.
entries.currentTake: The ability to choose where I live, how I work, who I spend time around, and what receives my attention matters enormously. I don’t think chronic stress can be separated cleanly from the structure of a life.
supportingDetails: Remove persistent stressors where possible instead of only becoming better at tolerating them.
Freedom is not the absence of commitment; it is room to respond honestly.

entries.title: Relationships Are Environment
entries.summary: The people around me are part of my nervous system’s daily habitat.
entries.currentTake: Connection, safety, friction, loneliness, play, and the quality of conversation are not soft extras. They change what a day feels like from the inside—and probably more of health than most protocol lists acknowledge.
supportingDetails: Notice who makes the system contract and who makes more of me available.
Belonging and solitude can both be medicine in the right dose.

entries.title: Light Is the Main Signal
entries.summary: A proper light environment is one of the highest-priority physical inputs in my health model.
entries.currentTake: I want bright, natural daytime light—especially early—and a real transition toward darkness at night. The body should not have to guess whether it is noon or midnight.
supportingDetails: Get outdoors early when possible; window light is not the same as being outside.
Let daytime be bright and evenings become progressively dimmer.
Treat screens and overhead light as part of the environment, not neutral objects.

entries.title: Less Screen, More World
entries.summary: I would benefit from spending less time inside screens and social-media feeds.
entries.currentTake: The problem is not only blue light. It is attention, comparison, fragmentation, posture, stillness, and replacing direct experience with an endless stream of representations.
supportingDetails: More periods with the phone physically elsewhere.
More boredom, walks, conversations, and unmediated surroundings.

entries.title: Nature and Ground Contact
entries.summary: I would ideally spend more time outdoors with bare feet directly on the Earth.
entries.currentTake: Even without settling every proposed electrical mechanism, natural light, uneven ground, open space, weather, and contact with the living world feel like a more appropriate human environment than climate-controlled boxes all day.
supportingDetails: Ordinary nature contact matters independently of any grounding theory.
The electrical explanation remains interesting to me and belongs in Frontiers.

entries.title: Resonance Breathing
entries.summary: 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out. About ten minutes first thing in the morning, usually looking out an open window.
entries.currentTake: This is simple enough to keep doing and useful enough that it has earned a place. I understand it as slow, resonance-style breathing: a steady rhythm that seems to help the system begin the day with less noise.
supportingDetails: Gentle rather than maximal breaths.
Buteyko’s emphasis on nasal breathing, less air, and CO₂ tolerance has also been broadly useful to me.
The point is a better default—not collecting breathwork techniques.

entries.title: Downshift on Purpose
entries.summary: Recovery sometimes needs an intentional doorway rather than waiting for exhaustion to win.
entries.currentTake: NSDR, NuCalm, quiet time, naps, and simply doing nothing can all help. I use NuCalm and consider these useful tools, but none needs to become a grand protocol.
supportingDetails: NuCalm has been in my toolkit for years.
NSDR is useful when sleep is not available or a full reset is needed.
Downtime is not a productivity failure.

entries.title: Make Night Feel Like Night
entries.summary: Sleep begins with the signals that precede it, not only the moment my head hits a pillow.
entries.currentTake: Darkness, quieter inputs, cooler air, fewer screens, and a reasonably consistent rhythm matter more to me than turning sleep into another optimization contest.
supportingDetails: Protect darkness and reduce unnecessary stimulation.
Use simple environmental changes before complicated sleep technology.

entries.title: Walking
entries.summary: I walk a lot. It’s probably the most reliable form of exercise in my life.
entries.currentTake: Walking gives me movement, outdoor time, orientation to a place, thinking space, and often daylight at the same time. Its ordinariness is part of why it works.
supportingDetails: Walk to understand a city.
Prefer movement that naturally fits inside life.

entries.title: Strength and Capacity
entries.summary: Strength keeps more of life available and is worth maintaining without making training the center of existence.
entries.currentTake: After fifteen years as a trainer, I still value basic resistance training, useful movement patterns, gradual progression, and enough muscle to remain capable. The best program is one that survives real life.
supportingDetails: Consistency beats the perfect theoretical program.
Train movement patterns and capacity, not only appearance.

entries.title: Aerobic Base + Hard Efforts
entries.summary: I’m not currently doing much structured cardio, and I think I would benefit from more.
entries.currentTake: If I were doing this closer to my ideal, I’d add a couple of easier aerobic-style sessions and one or two interval or harder-effort exposures each week. That is a direction, not a claim about my current routine.
supportingDetails: Most dedicated aerobic work can feel controlled rather than punishing.
Occasional harder efforts preserve a capacity daily walking does not fully train.

entries.title: Don’t Make Food Your Religion
entries.summary: Food matters. Food is not everything, and I don’t want eating to become an identity or a source of constant fear.
entries.currentTake: Nutrition sits inside a larger life. A theoretically perfect diet that creates anxiety, rigidity, social isolation, or endless mental overhead is not obviously producing wellbeing.
supportingDetails: Use principles without joining a diet tribe.
Notice what actually supports energy, digestion, mood, training, and enjoyment.

entries.title: Feed the Metabolism
entries.summary: My accumulated food model is broadly bioenergetic and Peat-adjacent, but flexible rather than doctrinal.
entries.currentTake: I lean toward eating enough, not unnecessarily fearing carbohydrates, getting adequate protein, choosing nutrient-dense foods, preferring traditional or saturated fats, and minimizing heavily processed seed oils where practical. Gelatin and collagen also make sense to me.
supportingDetails: Warmth, energy, digestion, mood, sleep, appetite, and training response are useful feedback.
Calories and protein matter, but permanent tracking usually does not.
This is a bias and a working model—not a rigid Ray Peat diet page.

entries.title: Biofield + Biofield Tuning
entries.summary: I think the biofield deserves to be treated as a serious part of the human picture, not dismissed because the prevailing model has trouble accounting for it.
entries.currentTake: Biofield Tuning gives me a practical way to engage with that model through sound and felt experience. I’m more convinced by the reality of the phenomenon than I am by every proposed mechanism or map around it.
supportingDetails: Experience and mechanism are separate questions.
The relationship among sound, electrical organization, memory, and physiology remains unusually interesting.

entries.title: Bioelectricity + Morphogenesis
entries.summary: The idea that living systems use bioelectric networks to coordinate form, repair, and collective intelligence may be far more important than most health conversations acknowledge.
entries.currentTake: Michael Levin’s work opens a different scale of question: not only what individual molecules do, but how living systems know what shape to build, what to repair, and what counts as the self.
supportingDetails: This is a research direction, not a personal protocol.
It may eventually connect Human to a deeper Browser rabbit hole.

entries.title: Light Biology
entries.summary: I think light is biological information, not merely illumination or a delivery system for vitamin D.
entries.currentTake: Circadian timing is only the beginning. Wavelength, intensity, darkness, infrared exposure, mitochondria, and the relationship between light and cellular water all seem worthy of much more attention.
supportingDetails: The conventional indoor light environment is historically strange.
Well-supported circadian effects and more speculative biophysical mechanisms should remain distinguishable.

entries.title: Structured / EZ Water
entries.summary: The water inside and alongside living structures may be doing considerably more than the standard hydration story suggests.
entries.currentTake: Gerald Pollack’s exclusion-zone work and the links people propose among interfacial water, charge, infrared light, and biology deserve investigation. I’m interested without pretending every extrapolation has been demonstrated.
supportingDetails: The laboratory phenomenon and whole-body health claims are different evidence questions.
This belongs near light biology and bioelectricity.

entries.title: EMF Biology
entries.summary: I think the biological effects of our electromagnetic environment are substantially underestimated.
entries.currentTake: Human biology developed inside natural electrical and magnetic conditions, not continuous close-range wireless exposure. Distance, duration, timing, and the sleep environment seem worth taking seriously without converting life into an exposure panic.
supportingDetails: Practical reduction can be simple: distance, airplane mode, hardwiring, and fewer devices near sleep.
The strongest claims still deserve careful source and counterargument review.

entries.title: Biological-Conflict Models
entries.summary: I don’t consider German New Medicine or biological decoding complete systems, but I think the conventional model is incomplete too.
entries.currentTake: The possibility that some symptoms are meaningful adaptive responses to conflict or overwhelming experience is worth investigating. Fixed organ-conflict maps and claims that replace medical care are a different matter.
supportingDetails: Curiosity about meaning should complement—not cancel—appropriate medical evaluation.
The most useful question may be: what else was happening when this began?

entries.title: Consciousness + Physiology
entries.summary: I’ve become increasingly convinced that consciousness, expectation, meaning, and physiology cannot be cleanly separated.
entries.currentTake: Placebo and nocebo effects, attention, intention, relational context, and reports of non-local effects all point toward a stranger relationship between mind and matter than the usual story allows. The size and mechanism of those effects remain open questions.
supportingDetails: Meaning effects are real even when a proposed quantum explanation is not.
Non-local consciousness deserves a serious rabbit hole, not a throwaway certainty.

entries.title: Altered-State Somatic Exploration
entries.summary: Intentional altered states have sometimes made bodily information available that my analytical mind could not access in the same way.
entries.currentTake: I’m interested in the capacity of carefully held altered states to change attention, sensation, spontaneous movement, and emotional processing. My experience is personal; it is not a universal protocol or an explanation for every symptom.
supportingDetails: Context, legality, safety, and individual response matter.
The experience can be meaningful without every interpretation being literally true.
